units.title: Complexity and correctness
units.blurb: Before any data structure, the language you use to judge one.

lesson.md:
Big-O does not measure time. It measures how the amount of work grows as the input grows.

That distinction is the whole topic. A stopwatch tells you about your laptop, your language and what else was running. Big-O tells you something that stays true on every machine that will ever exist.
Say a function does one unit of work per element. Ten elements, ten units. A thousand elements, a thousand units. Double the input, double the work. We call that O(n): the work is proportional to n.
O(n) does not mean "n operations". It means the work grows *in proportion to* n. A loop doing three things per element is still O(n), because tripling every step does not change how the curve bends.

This is why constants get dropped. O(3n) and O(n) describe the same shape, and shape is what survives a change of hardware. Buying a machine twice as fast halves your constant; it does nothing at all to the shape.

Constants still matter to your users. They just are not what Big-O is for. An O(n) algorithm with a huge constant can lose to an O(n log n) one on every input you actually have. Big-O is a claim about behaviour as n grows without limit.

quiz.stem: What does O(n) tell you about an algorithm?
options: It takes n seconds to run
Its work grows in proportion to the input size
It is faster than any O(n squared) algorithm
quiz.explain: Big-O describes growth, not duration and not an exact count. Proportional growth means doubling the input roughly doubles the work, whatever the machine.

misconception.0: reads Big-O as a measure of clock time rather than growth
misconception.1: reads O(n) as an exact operation count rather than a proportion
misconception.3: believes a lower complexity class always wins, regardless of input size or constants

quiz.stem: A loop over n elements does 5 operations per element. What is its complexity?
quiz.explain: Constant factors are dropped, so O(5n) simplifies to O(n). Five times the work per step scales the curve, it does not bend it.

misconception.0: keeps constant factors in the final notation
misconception.2: mistakes the per-element constant for the whole complexity
misconception.3: confuses a repeated factor with an exponent

quiz.stem: An O(n) algorithm is always faster in practice than an O(n squared) algorithm.
quiz.explain: Only for large enough n. With a big constant or a small input, the O(n squared) version can easily win. Big-O is a statement about the limit, not about your actual data.

misconception.0: treats asymptotic ordering as a guarantee at every input size

quiz.stem: How many times does the inner statement run, in terms of n?
quiz.explain: The inner loop is bounded by 3, not by n, so the total is 3n and the complexity is O(n). Nesting alone does not make something quadratic.

misconception.1: assumes any nested loop is quadratic without checking the inner bound
misconception.2: multiplies the constant into a quadratic term that is not there
misconception.3: counts loop depth rather than the work each loop actually does

quiz.stem: Why does Big-O deliberately ignore the speed of the machine?
options: Because all computers run at the same speed
Because hardware changes the constant factor but not the growth curve
Because Big-O is only used for theoretical algorithms
quiz.explain: A faster machine divides every step by the same factor. That moves the whole curve down, it does not change its shape, and shape is the thing that decides what happens as n grows.

misconception.0: misunderstands the abstraction as a claim about real hardware being uniform
misconception.2: sees complexity analysis as academic rather than a practical prediction
misconception.3: confuses profiling with asymptotic analysis

quiz.stem: Two loops run one after the other, the first n times and the second n times. What is the complexity?
quiz.explain: Sequential work adds: n + n = 2n, which is O(n). You multiply only when one loop runs inside another.

misconception.0: multiplies sequential loops instead of adding them
misconception.2: reaches for a familiar complexity class without deriving it
misconception.3: believes complexity cannot be determined without running the code

quiz.stem: What is the time complexity of reading the element at a known index of an array?
quiz.explain: The address is computed arithmetically from the start of the array, so the work is the same whether the array holds ten items or ten million.

misconception.1: imagines some search structure behind array indexing
misconception.2: thinks the array is scanned to reach the index
misconception.3: believes array access degrades with size

quiz.stem: An algorithm is O(n). Which statement is strictly correct?
options: Its work grows exactly in proportion to n
Its work grows at most in proportion to n, ignoring constants
Its work grows at least in proportion to n
It performs one operation per element
quiz.explain: Big-O is an upper bound. An algorithm that is O(n) may well be faster on some inputs. Theta describes an exact bound and Omega describes a lower one.

misconception.0: reads O as an exact bound, which is Theta
misconception.2: reads O as a lower bound, which is Omega
misconception.3: reads O(n) as a literal operation count

quiz.stem: Doubling the input of an O(n) algorithm multiplies the work by roughly ___.
quiz.explain: Proportional growth: twice the input, twice the work. Quadrupling would be O(n squared) behaviour.

misconception.1: applies quadratic scaling to a linear algorithm
misconception.2: applies constant-time scaling to a linear algorithm
misconception.3: confuses the growth factor with the input size itself

quiz.stem: You measure two functions on an input of 1,000 items. A takes 40 ms, B takes 12 ms. What can you conclude about their complexity?
options: B has lower complexity than A
A is O(n squared) and B is O(n)
Nothing, from a single input size
quiz.explain: Complexity is about the shape of the curve, and one point does not describe a curve. Measure across several input sizes and see how the times change; that is what reveals growth.

misconception.0: infers asymptotic class from a single timing measurement
misconception.1: assigns specific complexity classes from one data point
misconception.3: concludes equality from measurements that were not equal

lesson.md: Real code rarely does one clean thing. It sorts, then loops, then loops again. To get a single complexity out of that, you find the term that grows fastest and throw the rest away.

Suppose a function costs n squared + 100n + 5000 operations. At n = 10 the constant 5000 dominates completely. At n = 1,000,000 the n squared term is a million times larger than everything else combined. Big-O cares about the second case, so this is O(n squared).
Add when steps run one after another. Multiply when one runs inside another. Getting these the wrong way round is the most common analysis error there is.

The ordering you need, slowest-growing first:

O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n squared) < O(n cubed) < O(2 to the n) < O(n factorial)

quiz.stem: Simplify: n squared + 100n + 5000
quiz.explain: Only the fastest-growing term survives. For large n the squared term dwarfs the others, and lower terms are dropped along with constants.

misconception.1: keeps lower-order terms in the final notation
misconception.2: picks the largest number rather than the fastest-growing term
misconception.3: picks the term with the biggest coefficient rather than the biggest growth

quiz.stem: A function sorts the array, then scans it once. What is the overall complexity?
quiz.explain: n log n for the sort plus n for the scan is n log n + n, and n log n dominates. The scan is free in comparison.

misconception.0: ignores the cost of the sort
misconception.2: multiplies the sequential steps instead of adding them
misconception.3: confuses the sort's log factor with the whole cost

quiz.stem: How many times does work() run?
quiz.explain: The inner loop runs n times for each of the n outer iterations, so the counts multiply: n times n.

misconception.0: adds nested loops instead of multiplying them
misconception.2: reaches for n log n without deriving the count
misconception.3: counts only the outer loop

quiz.stem: Which of these grows fastest as n gets large?
quiz.explain: Exponential growth eventually overtakes every polynomial. At n = 50, 2 to the n is already larger than 50 cubed by a factor of over a trillion.

misconception.0: ranks by how complicated the expression looks rather than by growth rate
misconception.1: ranks by the exponent's appearance rather than by growth type
misconception.3: assumes the largest visible power wins, missing that the exponent is the variable

quiz.stem: Two loops, the first running n times and the second running m times, one after the other. What is the complexity?
quiz.explain: Sequential steps add, giving O(n + m). You cannot simplify to one variable, because n and m grow independently. O(max) is proportional to it but O(n + m) is the standard form.

misconception.0: multiplies sequential loops, treating them as nested
misconception.2: collapses two independent variables into one
misconception.3: drops a term that cannot be dropped when the variables are independent

quiz.stem: How many times does work() run, in terms of n?
options: about n squared over 2, which is O(n squared)
quiz.explain: The inner loop shortens each pass: n, then n-1, then n-2, summing to n(n+1)/2. Halving is a constant factor, so this is still O(n squared).

misconception.0: misses that the inner bound depends on i
misconception.2: assumes a shrinking inner loop must produce a log factor
misconception.3: adds the loops instead of summing the series

quiz.stem: Order these from slowest-growing to fastest-growing.
quiz.explain: Constant, then logarithmic, then linear, then quadratic. Knowing this ladder by heart is most of what complexity questions test.

quiz.stem: A loop over n elements calls a helper that is itself O(log n). What is the total?

code.java:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    binarySearch(a, i);   // O(log n)
code.python:
for i in range(n):
    binary_search(a, i)   # O(log n)

quiz.explain: Work inside a loop multiplies by the number of iterations: n times log n. The helper's cost is paid on every pass.

misconception.0: adds the nested cost instead of multiplying it
misconception.2: ignores the surrounding loop
misconception.3: assumes any nesting is quadratic without looking at the inner cost

quiz.stem: O(n squared + n) is a correct but non-standard way to write O(n squared).
quiz.explain: It is not wrong, merely unsimplified. Conventionally you reduce to the dominant term, exactly as you would not leave an answer as 4/8.

misconception.1: believes an unsimplified bound is incorrect rather than untidy

quiz.stem: Why is O(log n) so much better than O(n) at large scale?
options: Because logarithms are always small numbers
Because doubling n adds only one step, rather than doubling the work
Because it never examines the whole input
Because log n is a constant
quiz.explain: That is what a logarithm is. Going from a thousand to a million items adds about ten steps to a binary search, while a linear scan does a thousand times the work.

misconception.0: treats log n as small rather than slow-growing
misconception.2: confuses a property of some log-time algorithms with the reason
misconception.3: treats a slowly growing function as constant

lesson.md: Most complexity questions are answered by looking at how the loop variable changes. There are only a few shapes, and once you recognise them you stop having to think.
The variable is added to, so the loop runs n times. That is linear.

lesson.src: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)   // i++  ->  n steps  ->  O(n)

lesson.md: The variable is multiplied or divided, so the count is how many times you can double before passing n. That is logarithmic.

lesson.src: for (int i = 1; i < n; i = i * 2)   // 1,2,4,8...  ->  log n steps  ->  O(log n)

i = 1
while i < n:      # 1,2,4,8...
    i = i * 2     # O(log n)

lesson.md: Adding to the counter gives linear. Multiplying it gives logarithmic. That single rule answers most exam questions on the topic.
The base of the logarithm never appears in the notation. Changing base multiplies by a constant, and constants are dropped, so O(log base 2 of n) and O(log base 10 of n) are both written O(log n).

quiz.stem: What is the complexity of this loop?

code.java: for (int i = 1; i < n; i = i * 2) work();
code.python:
i = 1
while i < n:
    work()
    i = i * 2

quiz.explain: i doubles each pass, so it reaches n after about log base 2 of n steps. Multiplying the counter is the signature of logarithmic time.

misconception.0: counts any single loop as linear without reading how the counter changes
misconception.2: adds a factor of n that no enclosing loop provides
misconception.3: treats a loop that runs few times as constant

quiz.stem: What is the complexity of this loop?

code.java: for (int i = n; i > 0; i = i / 2) work();
code.python:
i = n
while i > 0:
    work()
    i = i // 2

quiz.explain: Halving reaches 1 in about log n steps. Dividing the counter is logarithmic for exactly the same reason that multiplying it is.

misconception.0: counts iterations as n because the loop starts at n
misconception.2: treats a single loop as quadratic, when nesting is what produces a square
misconception.3: keeps the constant factor, and misses that halving repeatedly is logarithmic rather than linear

quiz.stem: Why is the base of the logarithm left out of O(log n)?
options: Because changing base only multiplies by a constant, which is dropped
Because the base does not affect the number of steps
quiz.explain: log base 10 of n equals log base 2 of n divided by log base 2 of 10, a fixed factor. Constants are dropped, so the base disappears from the notation.

misconception.0: believes a convention rather than the mathematical reason
misconception.2: believes the base has no effect on the actual step count, when it changes it by a constant factor
misconception.3: has a gap in the underlying maths

quiz.stem: What is the complexity of this pair of loops?
quiz.explain: A linear outer loop containing a logarithmic inner loop multiplies to n log n. This is the shape of the good sorting algorithms.

misconception.0: assumes nested loops are quadratic without reading the inner counter
misconception.2: ignores the outer loop
misconception.3: ignores the inner loop

quiz.stem: What is the complexity of appending to the end of a fixed-capacity array?
quiz.explain: You write at a known index and increase the count. No part of that depends on how many items are already stored.

misconception.1: imagines a search structure behind a direct write
misconception.2: assumes the array must be traversed to find the end
misconception.3: assumes a quadratic cost where no repeated pass over the data exists

quiz.stem: What is the complexity of inserting at the front of an array, shifting everything right?
quiz.explain: Every existing element moves one place, so the work is proportional to how many there are. This is precisely the weakness a linked list is designed to fix.

misconception.0: assumes all array writes are constant time regardless of shifting
misconception.1: imagines a search or index structure behind a simple shift of elements
misconception.3: double counts the single shifting pass

quiz.stem: Roughly how many times does work() run when n is 1,000,000?

code.java: for (int i = 1; i < n; i = i * 2) work();
code.python:
i = 1
while i < n:
    work()
    i = i * 2

quiz.explain: 2 to the 20 is just over a million, so doubling from 1 reaches a million in about twenty steps. That gap between twenty and a million is why logarithmic time matters.

misconception.1: estimates the square root instead of the logarithm
misconception.2: reads the loop as linear
misconception.3: halves n instead of taking its logarithm

quiz.stem: A loop runs n times and calls a function that itself loops n times. What is the complexity?
quiz.explain: Complexity does not care whether the nesting is written inline or hidden behind a call. Always look inside the functions you call.

misconception.0: counts only the visible loop and ignores the callee's cost
misconception.1: adds the callee's cost instead of multiplying by the iterations
misconception.3: assumes a log factor that nothing in the code produces

quiz.stem: What is the complexity of this loop?
quiz.explain: The inner loop is fixed at 1000 no matter how large n gets, so it is a constant factor: O(1000n) is O(n). Slow in practice, linear in shape.

misconception.1: keeps the constant in the final notation
misconception.2: treats every nested loop as quadratic
misconception.3: treats a constant bound as if it grew with n

quiz.stem: Which loop shape produces O(n log n)?
options: A loop that halves the counter, inside a loop that halves the counter
A loop that increments, inside a loop that increments
A loop that doubles the counter, inside a loop that increments
A single loop that doubles the counter
quiz.explain: n iterations outside, log n inside, multiplied. That is the shape of merge sort and heap sort.

misconception.0: gives log squared, by nesting two logarithmic loops
misconception.1: gives quadratic, by nesting two linear loops
misconception.3: gives plain logarithmic, with no enclosing linear loop

lesson.md: Time is not the only resource. Space complexity asks how much extra memory an algorithm needs as the input grows, and it is counted the same way: growth, constants dropped.
The word that matters is *extra*. The input itself is normally not counted, because you were given it. What counts is what you allocate on top.

Recursion is not free. Every pending call keeps a frame on the call stack, so a recursion n deep costs O(n) space even when the function allocates nothing at all. This is the single most missed source of space cost.
This is also why deep recursion crashes with a stack overflow while an equivalent loop runs happily. The loop keeps one frame; the recursion keeps n.

quiz.stem: What is the extra space complexity of finding the maximum with a single variable?
quiz.explain: One variable, regardless of input size. The input array is not counted as extra space because you did not allocate it.

misconception.1: assumes some hidden structure grows with the input
misconception.2: counts the input array as extra space
misconception.3: reads a quadratic cost into a single pass that stores nothing

quiz.stem: What is the space complexity of this function?
quiz.explain: A new array proportional to the input is allocated, so the extra space grows with n.

misconception.0: counts only scalar variables and overlooks the allocated array
misconception.2: confuses the single allocation with a nested one
misconception.3: assumes a logarithmic cost where a full copy is being allocated

quiz.stem: What is the space complexity of this recursion?
quiz.explain: n calls are alive at once, each holding a stack frame. Allocating nothing explicitly does not make a recursion free.

misconception.0: believes recursion costs no space because no allocation is written
misconception.1: assumes recursion depth is logarithmic when nothing is being divided
misconception.3: multiplies recursion depth by itself instead of counting frames once per level

quiz.stem: An iterative loop and an equivalent recursion always use the same amount of space.
quiz.explain: The loop reuses one frame; the recursion keeps one per pending call. That is exactly why deep recursion overflows the stack and the loop does not.

misconception.0: does not account for the call stack when comparing the two

quiz.stem: A balanced binary tree of n nodes is traversed recursively. What is the space complexity?
quiz.explain: The stack holds one frame per level, and a balanced tree is about log n levels deep. An unbalanced tree degrades to O(n), which is the case worth remembering.

misconception.0: forgets the call stack entirely
misconception.2: counts one frame per node rather than per level
misconception.3: multiplies node count by depth

quiz.stem: Why is the input array usually excluded from space complexity?
options: Because arrays are stored outside memory
Because it measures extra space the algorithm allocates, not what it was handed
Because the input is always small
quiz.explain: The convention isolates the algorithm's own cost. Two algorithms solving the same problem receive the same input, so counting it would tell you nothing that distinguishes them.

misconception.0: has a gap in how memory works
misconception.2: assumes something about input size that no analysis assumes
misconception.3: believes an array of n elements takes constant space

quiz.stem: What is the space complexity here?
quiz.explain: Time is O(n squared) but space is O(n): one array of n booleans, allocated once. Looping over a structure repeatedly does not allocate it repeatedly.

misconception.0: overlooks the allocated array
misconception.2: reads the time complexity as the space complexity
misconception.3: adds a dimension to the space cost that no third allocation creates

quiz.stem: An algorithm is O(n) time and O(1) space. What does that mean in practice?
options: It reads each element once and keeps only a fixed number of variables
It is faster than any O(n log n) algorithm
It uses no memory at all
quiz.explain: One pass, a handful of running variables. Two pointers and running-sum techniques both live in this shape, which is why they are so prized.

misconception.1: conflates a space bound with a guarantee about speed
misconception.2: reads O(1) space as zero memory rather than constant memory
misconception.3: invents a constraint that the notation does not express

quiz.stem: Trading extra memory for less time is a standard technique.
quiz.explain: It has a name: the space-time tradeoff. A hash set turns an O(n squared) scan into an O(n) one by spending O(n) memory, which is most of what the hashing unit is about.

misconception.1: has not yet met the tradeoff that underpins hashing and dynamic programming

quiz.stem: What is the space complexity of this recursion?
quiz.explain: n halves each call, so the recursion is about log n deep and holds that many frames. Depth is what determines recursive space, not the number of calls made overall.

misconception.0: forgets the call stack
misconception.2: assumes all recursion is linear in depth without reading how the argument shrinks
misconception.3: multiplies the depth by n, when only the depth occupies the stack

lesson.md: One algorithm can have several complexities, depending on what the input looks like. A linear search finds the target immediately if it is first, and scans everything if it is last or absent.

Best case is the luckiest input. Worst case is the unluckiest. Average case is what happens across typical inputs. When someone states a complexity without qualifying it, they almost always mean the worst case, because that is the only one that is a promise.

Amortised is not the average case. Average case is about which input you happen to get. Amortised is about the cost of one operation spread across a long sequence of operations, and it holds even for the unluckiest sequence.

A dynamic array is the standard example. Appending is usually O(1), but when it fills up it allocates a bigger array and copies everything, which is O(n). Because it doubles, that expensive copy happens rarely enough that the cost per append averages to a constant. Appending is O(1) amortised.
Hash table lookup is the reverse warning: O(1) average, but O(n) worst case when everything collides into one bucket. Quoting only the average hides a real failure mode.

quiz.stem: What is the best case for a linear search?
quiz.explain: The target is the first element you check, so you return after one comparison.

misconception.1: confuses linear search with binary search
misconception.2: reports the worst case when asked for the best
misconception.3: reads a nested cost into a single scan

quiz.stem: What is the worst case for a linear search?
quiz.explain: The target is last, or missing entirely, so every element is examined.

misconception.0: reports the best case when asked for the worst
misconception.1: confuses linear search with binary search, which needs sorted input
misconception.3: reads a nested cost into a single scan

quiz.stem: When a complexity is quoted without saying which case, which is normally meant?
quiz.explain: The worst case is the only one that is a guarantee. Best case describes one lucky input and promises nothing.

misconception.0: assumes the most flattering figure is the convention
misconception.2: assumes typical behaviour is the default claim
misconception.3: conflates amortised analysis with the default convention

quiz.stem: What does it mean that appending to a dynamic array is O(1) amortised?
options: Appends are constant on average across a sequence, with occasional O(n) resizes
Appends are constant only for typical inputs
Appending is constant only when the array is not full
quiz.explain: Individual appends can be O(n) when a resize happens, but doubling makes those rare enough that the cost per append averages to a constant over any long sequence.

misconception.0: reads amortised as a guarantee about every single operation
misconception.2: conflates amortised with average case over inputs
misconception.3: describes the fast path but misses that amortised analysis includes the resize

quiz.stem: Amortised complexity and average-case complexity mean the same thing.
quiz.explain: Average case is over the distribution of inputs. Amortised is over a sequence of operations and holds even for the worst possible sequence, which makes it a much stronger claim.

misconception.0: treats amortised and average case as interchangeable, the classic exam trap on this topic

quiz.stem: What is the worst case for looking up a key in a hash table?
quiz.explain: If every key collides into one bucket the lookup degrades to scanning a list of n items. O(1) is the average case, not a promise.

misconception.0: quotes the average case as though it were the worst
misconception.1: confuses a hash table with a balanced tree
misconception.3: overstates the collision cost, which is one bucket scan rather than a nested one

quiz.stem: Why is the worst case usually the one worth quoting?
options: It is the easiest to calculate
It is the only one that guarantees behaviour on every input
It is always the same as the average case
Best case is impossible to determine
quiz.explain: A worst-case bound is a promise nothing can break. The other cases describe what tends to happen, which is no use when an adversary or an unlucky data set picks your input.

misconception.0: picks convenience as the reason rather than the guarantee
misconception.2: believes the cases usually coincide, when they often differ sharply
misconception.3: believes best case is undecidable

quiz.stem: Quicksort's average case is O(n log n). What is its worst case?
quiz.explain: With a bad pivot every time, each partition removes only one element, giving n levels of n work. This is why real implementations randomise or median-select the pivot.

misconception.0: assumes average and worst coincide
misconception.1: quotes a bound better than the average, which cannot be a worst case
misconception.3: treats a bad pivot as exponential, when it degrades to a quadratic number of comparisons

quiz.stem: A sorted array is searched with binary search. What is the best case?
options: O(1), the middle element is the target
quiz.explain: The first probe lands on the target, so it returns immediately. The worst case is the familiar O(log n).

misconception.1: reports the worst case when asked for the best
misconception.2: confuses binary search with linear search
misconception.3: quotes the cost of sorting rather than of searching an already sorted array

quiz.stem: You need a hard guarantee on response time. Which figure should you design against?
quiz.explain: Only the worst case bounds every input. Amortised is close, but it bounds a sequence rather than any individual operation, so a single call can still be slow.

misconception.0: designs a guarantee against the luckiest possible input
misconception.1: designs a guarantee against typical behaviour
misconception.3: believes an amortised bound constrains each individual operation
